War room standard

Project 38 · the standard every war room in this repository follows · index · repo randomcase/war-room-standard

A war room is a template. One JSON file under templates-war/, one page under projects/, rendered by session-index.mjs; the fields below are the standard. The ending is the fixed point: the room is built backward from it, and the computer’s job is to reach the ending from the numbers and say by how much it missed.

FieldShapeRule
id, kind, orderstring, "war-room", numberthe file’s name, its kind, and its place
name, also, theatrestringswhat it is called, what else it is called, where it was
from, toISO datesthe opening and the ending; the ending is fixed — for Vietnam it is the Fall of Saigon, 1975-04-30, and nothing after it belongs in the room
respondsToid, optionala room that answers another room
sides[]side, who, backedtwo or more
chain[]who, role, from, to, didthe chain of command, one line item per person; presidents get one each
phases[]from, to, name, textthree to five
gaugeunit, series[[x, v]]one number that rises and falls, by year or by date
predictionending, endingName, unit, series, fitFrom, marks, noteoptional; the computer fits a line to the series from fitFrom and reports the zero date and its error against the ending. The note says what the numbers cannot see. The computer complies with the numbers; the note is the only place a person may disagree with it
days[][date, side, text]optional; a spread, one line per day, back and forth between the sides; fifty days where fifty can be had, and lives where they cannot
cost[]k, vwhat it cost, each side
outcomestringone paragraph
open[]stringswhat is still argued
sources[]stringswhere the numbers come from
text, wovenBystringsthe ship’s own fields, as every template has

The American standard

Four U.S. presidents primarily managed American involvement in the Vietnam War, and each gets one line item and one repository in this index. A fifth presided over the ending and is listed as such.

#PresidentTermLine item
1Dwight D. Eisenhower1953–1961Managed early involvement: refused to intervene at Dien Bien Phu, declined to sign the Geneva Accords, built the Diem government, and sent the first military advisers.
2John F. Kennedy1961–1963Managed early involvement: turned the adviser mission into a 16,000-man shadow army with helicopters and Special Forces, refused the combat troops his advisers asked for in 1961, and approved the coup that removed Diem.
3Lyndon B. Johnson1963–1969Oversaw the massive escalation: the Tonkin Gulf resolution, Rolling Thunder, the first Marines at Da Nang, and over 500,000 combat troops in country by 1968. Announced a partial bombing halt and his own withdrawal from the 1968 race on the same night.
4Richard Nixon1969–1974Vietnamization: began pulling US troops out while shifting the fighting to the South Vietnamese army; widened the air war into Cambodia and Laos; signed the Paris Peace Accords; resigned twenty months before Saigon fell.
endingGerald Ford1974–1977Presided over the Fall of Saigon. Not one of the four who managed the war; the one who managed its ending: asked Congress for the aid Nixon had promised in private, was refused, and ordered the evacuation.

The Joint Chiefs

The chiefs are listed with their presidents. A chief who served two presidents appears once, with the first, and is given nothing more with the second except the duty he owed him. The five chiefs seated at the opening (1955-11-01) and the five at the fall (1975-04-30) each get a repository, projects 45–54.
